title: Y562 (Jixing) Black Box
before:
Y562 is a named export recipe of the Yunnan Tea Import and Export Company, sold under Jixing, meaning fortune, the company’s export brand. In the old coding the Y marks the company and the number stands for leaf grade and factory. A grade of five to six points to fine, tender leaf, unlike the coarse leaf in ripe bricks from the same years. The leaf came from Menghai.

It was made as ripe pu’er. The pile was developed to give, in weeks, what Hong Kong and Guangdong drinkers knew from raw pu’er aged for years. This lot dates from 1993, twenty years after Yunnan’s state factories brought wet piling into production. It was kept loose in a box rather than pressed, and has spent the years since in dry storage in Hong Kong. At thirty-three years it is well past the ten the trade counts for aged ripe pu’er, where storage shapes the leaf as much as time does.

title: Naka Gushu
scope: Approved village wording. Cake and type come from Stock.
before:
Naka is a Lahu village in the north of Mengsong, a township on the east side of Menghai County. The village lies near Huazhu Liangzi, the highest peak in Xishuangbanna, and the Liusha River runs between Mengsong and neighbouring Nannuo.

This leaf was made into ripe pu’er. Sun-dried leaf was wetted and heaped in a covered wet pile, where the microbes’ own heat worked on it and weekly turning let air through, then dried and pressed into a cake. The pile was developed to reach in weeks what raw pu’er takes years of aging to reach, so this cake is ready to drink now.

title: Yiwu Gushu
scope: Stock records Yiwu, a ripe cake and 2008. Tree age and pre-press aging are omitted.
before:
The leaf in this cake dates to 2008, and it had already been aging before it was pressed, so the cake began further along than one pressed from fresh leaf. It is gushu, leaf picked from trees far older than the bushes of a plantation, grown in the Yiwu tea area of eastern Xishuangbanna. Yiwu can name a township, a market centre or a much wider tea area, so the label speaks for a region rather than one village. The town grew into a gathering point for leaf from the old Six Famous Tea Mountains.

This leaf was made into ripe pu’er: wetted and heaped in a covered fermenting pile, where the heat of its own microbes darkens it in weeks, so it can be drunk without years of waiting. Yunnan’s state factories brought the pile into production in 1973, which places 2008 leaf in the style’s fourth decade. At eighteen years it counts as aged ripe pu’er. The leaf keeps changing with the air and moisture around it, so storage has shaped this cake as much as time.

title: Ripe Puerh Brick
scope: Stock records Yunnan, 1990 and brick. Wet piling describes the tea type.
before:
This brick of ripe pu’er was made from Yunnan leaf in 1990 and spent the decades since in Guangzhou’s tea trade. That is close to where the style began: the pile was devised to give, in weeks, the cup that Guangdong and Hong Kong drinkers knew from raw pu’er aged for years. Yunnan’s state factories brought wet piling into production in 1973, after a joint team studied faster piling in Guangdong, so this brick comes from the style’s second decade.

At thirty-six years it is well past the ten that mark aged ripe pu’er. The leaf keeps changing slowly with the air and moisture around it, which is why its storage has shaped it as much as its age.

title: Pasha Village
scope: The source describes aroma development with storage. It gives no trade-wide ten-year cutoff.
before: At eleven years it has passed the ten-year mark the trade uses for aged ripe pu’er.

title: Aged Northern Vietnam Ripe Pu-erh Tea
scope: Stock records loose ripe tea from the northern Vietnam highlands near Yunnan. Wet piling describes the tea type.
before:
This tea comes from the highlands of northern Vietnam, where the mountains run on into Yunnan. For generations, tea houses in Hong Kong and Guangzhou bought leaf from this side of the border and piled it in the pu’er way. This lot follows that line.

It was made into ripe pu’er. The leaf was wetted and heaped in a warm pile, which was covered to hold in the heat its own microbes give off and turned now and then to let in air. That way weeks do the change that raw pu’er needs years of ageing to reach. Afterwards it was aged loose rather than pressed.

title: Xiniu Tang Gushu
scope: Stock records the Chinese name, ripe type and cake form. The structured Yiwu origin is a separate evidence decision.
before:
This cake comes from Yiwu, in Yunnan. Its leaf was made into ripe pu’er, then pressed.

Before pressing, the sun-dried leaf was wetted and heaped into a fermenting pile. The microbes in the pile make their own heat, so the heap is covered to hold that heat in. It is turned about once a week to spread it and let in air, and it is kept below the point where the leaf would char. After one to two months the leaf is dried. The pile was developed to do in weeks what years of ageing did for raw pu’er in Hong Kong and Guangdong, so this cake is ready to drink now rather than after a long wait.
